nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the lyric, the riddle and the poetry of the inner life
literary_identity: Poet; one of the two or three greatest lyric poets in English, and the central woman poet of the nineteenth century.
biography: Born in Amherst, Massachusetts, on 10 December 1830, the daughter of a lawyer and congressman; she was educated at Amherst Academy and Mount Holyoke Female Seminary, which she left after a year. She lived almost entirely in her father's house, increasingly withdrawn after 1861, dressed in white, and conducted her closest relationships by letter. She wrote nearly 1,800 poems, sewn into fascicles, and published fewer than a dozen in her lifetime. She died in Amherst on 15 May 1886; the first collection appeared in 1890.
literary_profile: Dickinson wrote the lyric of extreme compression: her poems are short, usually rhymed in ballad or hymn stanzas, and organised around a single image or a riddle that the reader must solve. She writes about death, immortality, the mind, nature, love and fame with a wit and a metaphysical daring unmatched in American poetry, and her dashes, capitals and slant rhymes create a syntax of hesitation that is entirely her own.
stylistic_characteristics: Hymn and ballad measures broken by slant rhyme and irregular stress; dashes in place of punctuation; capitalised nouns; riddling circumlocution for the central subject; paradox and irony; the poem as a single compressed argument.
intellectual_concerns: Death and immortality; the mind and its power; nature and the seasons; love, renunciation and absence; religious doubt and the Calvinist inheritance; fame, publication and the woman artist.
historical_significance: Dickinson is one of the greatest poets in English and the founder of a distinctively American lyric of the inward life: her influence on twentieth-century poetry is as large as Whitman's, and the recovery of her manuscripts has made her a central figure in the criticism of gender, religion and American poetics.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the anti-slavery novel and the regional sketch
literary_identity: Novelist and abolitionist; the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, the most influential novel ever published in the United States.
biography: Born at Litchfield, Connecticut, on 14 June 1811, the daughter of the evangelical reformer Lyman Beecher; she was educated at her sister Catharine's Hartford Female Seminary and moved with the family to Cincinnati in 1832, where she married the clergyman and biblical scholar Calvin Stowe in 1836 and lived for eighteen years on the border of the slave state of Kentucky. Uncle Tom's Cabin was serialised in 1851-52 and published as a book in 1852; she wrote some thirty more books and died at Hartford on 1 July 1896.
literary_profile: Stowe wrote the novel as a moral instrument: Uncle Tom's Cabin is built for conversion, moving from comic domesticity to scenes of almost unbearable suffering, and its sentimental method was the most effective political rhetoric of the century. She was also a superb regional writer, and her New England village sketches and her novels of Calvinist households are the finest fictional record of nineteenth-century New England domestic life.
stylistic_characteristics: Sentimental tableaux designed to produce tears and conversion; dialect speech, black and Yankee; direct address to the reader; comic domestic dialogue; scriptural quotation and hymn; abrupt shifts of tone from comedy to martyrdom.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery and its destruction of families; Christian faith under persecution; the moral responsibility of the North; domesticity and the home as a moral unit; Calvinism and conversion; women's moral authority.
historical_significance: Uncle Tom's Cabin is the most influential novel in American history: it sold 300,000 copies in its first year in the United States and a million in Britain, was translated into more than sixty languages, and is credited by Lincoln's reported remark with starting the Civil War. It is a founding text of the American novel, of abolitionist literature and of the literature of human rights.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: The Mayflower; or, Sketches of Scenes and Characters among the Descendants of the Pilgrims (1843); Uncle Tom's Cabin; or, Life among the Lowly (1852); A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin (1853); Sunny Memories of Foreign Lands (1854); Dred: A Tale of the Great Dismal Swamp (1856); The Minister's Wooing (1859); The Pearl of Orr's Island (1862); Agnes of Sorrento (1862); Oldtown Folks (1869); Pink and White Tyranny (1871); My Wife and I (1871); Palmetto-Leaves (1873); Uncle Tom's Cabin on the American Stage (adaptations, 1850s); Poganuc People: Their Loves and Lives (1878).

birthplace: Cordova, Talbot County, Maryland, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the slave narrative, the oration and the political essay
literary_identity: Orator, editor and autobiographer; the greatest African-American writer of the nineteenth century and the most eloquent voice of the abolitionist movement.
biography: Born Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey in Talbot County, Maryland, in February 1818; he was enslaved until 1838, when he escaped to New York disguised as a sailor, and took the name Douglass. He spoke for the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society from 1841, published his Narrative in 1845, founded and edited the North Star in Rochester (1847-51), and after the Civil War held federal appointments in Haiti and Washington. He wrote three autobiographies and died in Washington on 20 February 1895.
literary_profile: Douglass wrote the American language of freedom: his Narrative is the classic slave narrative, built on the movement from ignorance to literacy to liberty, and his oratory — the Fourth of July address of 1852, 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' — is the greatest American political speech of the century. His prose is lucid, cadenced and controlled, and it turns the language of the Declaration against the republic that betrayed it.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person narrative of escape and self-making; direct oratorical address; biblical and constitutional quotation turned to indictment; irony and sarcasm; exact documentary detail of slavery's economy.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery and the destruction of the self; literacy and the awakening of freedom; the hypocrisy of American democracy; the Constitution and natural rights; Reconstruction and the failure of emancipation; the position of black women.
historical_significance: Douglass is the central African-American writer of the nineteenth century and one of the great prose writers in the language: his Narrative is the founding text of the African-American literary tradition, his Fourth of July oration is a permanent indictment of American hypocrisy, and his life made him the most photographed and most widely heard black man of his century.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845); The North Star (editor, 1847-51); Frederick Douglass' Paper (editor, 1851-60); 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the slave narrative and the literature of the fugitive woman
literary_identity: Writer and abolitionist; the author of Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, the first full-length slave narrative written by a woman.
biography: Born into slavery in Edenton, North Carolina, in 1813; she was taught to read by her mistress and, after her mother's death, was taken into the household of Dr James Norcom, whose sexual pursuit she escaped by hiding for seven years in a small garret above her grandmother's shed. She escaped to the North in 1842, was freed in 1852, worked as a nursemaid in New York and as a relief worker among the freedpeople in Virginia during and after the Civil War. She died in Washington in March 1897.
literary_profile: Jacobs wrote the slave narrative as a woman's testimony: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl tells what the male narratives could not — the sexual exploitation of enslaved women, the destruction of motherhood, and the cost of protecting a daughter's honour — and it does so in a controlled, ironic first person that addresses a white female readership directly. It is the founding text of African-American women's autobiography.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person retrospective narrative with direct appeal to the reader; the concealment of the narrator's name and identity; scenes of domestic terror and comic endurance; the seven-year hiding as a central emblem; plain documentary prose with a strong ironic edge.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery and sexual exploitation; motherhood and the sale of children; the cult of true womanhood and its exclusion of black women; concealment, literacy and self-defence; the North and the Fugitive Slave Law; Christian hypocrisy.
historical_significance: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl is a founding text of African-American women's writing and of American autobiography: it is the first slave narrative to make the sexual abuse of enslaved women its central subject, and its account of the seven-year hiding is one of the most extraordinary documents in American literature. Long read as fiction, it was authenticated as autobiography in the 1980s and is now canonical.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, Written by Herself (1861, as Linda Brent; ed. Lydia Maria Child); Letters and relief work among the freedpeople (1862-68, in the American Freedman).

literary_identity: Novelist, editor and the most commercially successful of the sensation novelists.
biography: Born in London on 4 October 1835, the daughter of a solicitor's clerk whose family broke up when she was young. She went on the stage in 1856 and acted with Edmund Falconer's company until 1860, when she turned to fiction. Lady Audley's Secret, serialised in Robin Goodfellow and then in the Sixpenny Magazine in 1861-62, made her famous; she founded and edited Belgravia (1866-76) and ran a large household at Richmond with her publisher John Maxwell, whose five children she raised before marrying him in 1874. She wrote more than eighty novels and died at Richmond on 4 February 1915.
literary_profile: Braddon took the machinery of the sensation novel — the secret, the grave, the locked room, the woman with a past — and made it the vehicle of a sustained argument about the position of women under the marriage law. Lady Audley is not a monster but a woman with no legal existence of her own, and the novel's famous question (is she mad, or only poor?) is answered by the Victorian asylum. Braddon wrote at speed and to a market, but her best books are technically adroit and socially sharp: she invented the professional woman writer as a commercial operator and made the sensation novel a woman's genre.
stylistic_characteristics: Rapid, incident-packed serial plotting; the big secret withheld to the last chapter; the ordinary domestic interior hiding a crime; a cool, ironic narrating voice; comedy of manners beside melodrama; the woman's viewpoint on marriage, money and the law.
intellectual_concerns: Marriage, bigamy and the legal non-existence of wives; madness and the asylum as instruments of family control; class, governesses and the genteel poor; money and the marriage market; theatricality and self-invention; the professional woman writer.
historical_significance: Braddon was the most widely read novelist in Britain in the 1860s and the central figure of the sensation vogue after Collins: she made the genre a woman's form, ran a magazine, and built a career independent of any male protector. Feminist criticism from the 1970s onward recovered Lady Audley's Secret as a serious analysis of the legal position of women, and Braddon is now canonical in Victorian fiction studies.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Gothic and the tale of terror
literary_identity: Novelist, short-story writer and journalist; the finest Irish writer of the supernatural tale before Stoker.
biography: Born in Dublin on 28 August 1814, the son of a Church of Ireland chaplain and the grand-nephew of Richard Brinsley Sheridan. He was educated at Trinity College Dublin and called to the bar in 1839, but abandoned law for journalism; he owned and edited the Dublin University Magazine and later the Dublin Evening Mail, and after the death of his wife Susanna in 1858 he withdrew from society and wrote at night. He produced the sensation novels of the 1860s and the supernatural tales collected in In a Glass Darkly (1872). He died in Dublin on 7 February 1873.
literary_profile: Le Fanu is the great Irish master of the Gothic after Maturin: his subject is the return of the past into the respectable present, and his method is the slow accumulation of documentary detail — the case notes of Dr Hesselius, the old family papers, the remembered rumour — until the supernatural becomes unavoidable. He wrote ghost stories as a scholar of the occult, with a precise sense of the psychology of fear, and his women (Carmilla, Maud Ruthyn, Madame de la Rougierre) are among the most disturbing in Victorian fiction.
stylistic_characteristics: The 'case' narrative framed by a medical or antiquarian editor; precise domestic detail followed by an irruption of the impossible; the haunted house, the old family, the revenant; a rich, deliberate prose; an oppressive sense of place, especially the Irish midlands and Dublin.
intellectual_concerns: The past returning on the present; ancestral guilt, secret marriages and disputed inheritance; the supernatural as psychological truth; the vulnerability of young women in a corrupt household; the Irish landscape and its folklore; religious dread and the Church of Ireland conscience.
historical_significance: Le Fanu is the central Irish Gothic novelist between Maturin and Stoker and the most important writer of the English supernatural tale before Henry James. 'Carmilla' (1872) is the founding text of the lesbian vampire narrative and a direct influence on Dracula; Uncle Silas is one of the great novels of suspense in English, and his work was admired by Yeats, M. R. James and Elizabeth Bowen.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the documentary and sensation novel
literary_identity: Novelist and dramatist; the Victorian pioneer of the documentary novel and of the fiction of social reform.
biography: Born at Ipsden, Oxfordshire, on 8 June 1814, the son of a landowner; he was educated at Magdalen College, Oxford, where he held a fellowship from 1842, and was called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn in 1843. He wrote plays, beginning with The Ladies' Battle (1849) and Masks and Faces (with Tom Taylor, 1852), and turned to fiction with Peg Woffington (1853). He researched his novels by collecting newspaper cuttings, visiting prisons, workhouses and factories, and corresponding with experts, and he campaigned in fiction against private lunatic asylums and for prison reform. He died in London on 11 April 1884.
literary_profile: Reade is the inventor of the English documentary novel: he called his method 'fictional history' and built his books out of verified cases, newspaper reports, blue books and personal investigation. The result is a fiction of argument and exposure — the private asylum in Hard Cash, the prison system in It Is Never Too Late to Mend — combined with a melodramatic power that made him one of the most popular novelists of the 1860s. The Cloister and the Hearth is the finest English historical novel of the fifteenth century and a deliberate answer to the romance of Scott.
stylistic_characteristics: The dossier method: documents, letters, newspaper extracts and trial evidence worked into narrative; violent melodramatic climaxes; polemic and reformist anger; a huge, crowded canvas; dialogue in period and dialect; the alternation of comedy and outrage.
intellectual_concerns: The abuse of institutional power (asylums, prisons, factories); the law and its failures; the condition of England and the two nations; religious controversy and the Reformation; love against money and class; the ethics of the writer as investigator.
historical_significance: Reade is the founding figure of the English novel of documented fact and a major influence on Zola's naturalism and on the twentieth-century documentary novel: Hard Cash helped to expose the private asylum scandals and It Is Never Too Late to Mend the prison system. The Cloister and the Hearth remains the classic English historical novel of the Burgundian fifteenth century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the sensation and marriage-question novel
literary_identity: Novelist; a best-selling 'daring' writer of the 1860s whose later fiction became a sharp comedy of manners.
biography: Born at Denbigh, north Wales, on 29 November 1840, the daughter of a clergyman and the niece of Sheridan Le Fanu, who encouraged her first stories. Her first novel, Cometh Up as a Flower (1867), was a sensation: a frank, first-person narrative of a woman's love and death that made her famous and notorious. She wrote twenty-six novels over more than forty years and lived latterly at Oxford, where she was a friend of Henry James and a celebrated talker. She died at Headington Hill, Oxford, on 5 June 1920.
literary_profile: Broughton began as a 'fast' novelist for the circulating libraries — her heroines desire, speak their minds and die of love — and became, in her later books, a cool and witty observer of the English marriage market. She was one of the first women novelists to write in the first person about female sexual feeling, and her best work combines the sensation plot with a genuinely modern irony about courtship and money.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person female narration with direct address to the reader; sentimental climax and ironic deflation; lively dialogue; the marriage market as a comic and cruel spectacle; a vein of self-mockery about the novelist's own trade.
intellectual_concerns: Marriage, courtship and the position of women; female desire and its punishment; money and the gentry; the contrast between provincial and London society; ageing, widowhood and the comedy of the older generation.
historical_significance: Broughton was one of the most popular and controversial woman novelists of the 1860s and a bridge from the sensation novel to the New Woman fiction of the 1890s: her frankness about women's desire opened ground that later writers could occupy, and her late novels were admired by Henry James and by the writers of the 1890s.
